where: every card body at 1152px — the page intro, the sibling-family paragraph, the two coloured strips, the definition list, and the Added / Merged badges on the Dov Halevy and Beatriz Salgado cards
finding: The card stretches to the full content column but nothing inside it was composed for that width, so the card fails in two directions at once. Prose is set to the entire measure: the page intro is one 1023px line of ~141 characters, the sibling explanation runs ~150 characters and then rags to a 217px second line, the failure strip is one 847px line of ~139 characters. Facts are set to phone width: the whole 'Brought by / Phone' block is 181px of content floating in a 1120px band. And the badges are pinned to the far right of their rows, roughly 900px from the names they qualify — 'Added' sits at x=1327 while 'Noa Halevy · 8th grade' ends at x=412, with a thousand pixels of nothing between the label and its subject. The reader pays twice: lines too long to track back on, and a badge whose tie to a child has been severed by the layout. Squinted, the right two-thirds of every card is empty except two floating pills, which reads as an unfinished layout rather than a composed one.
evidence: Measured on review--desktop-full.png: card inner width 272→1392. Intro paragraph x257–1279 on one line. Sibling paragraph line 1 x275–1355, line 2 x275–491. Amber strip text x285–1389 on one line. dl content x273–470 total. 'Added' badge x1327–1382 against name text ending x412; 'Merged' x1320–1382 against name ending x436. Nothing at all sits between x=470 and x=1320 in four of the five cards.
direction: At pointer widths the card should compose to the width it has been given rather than inherit the phone stack unchanged: prose bounded to a measure a reader can track (the intro and the sibling paragraph are both single sentences that want a column, not a band), the guardian facts and the child list able to sit beside each other rather than under each other, and the badge travelling with the name it labels instead of with the row's right edge.

where: the red strip on the Dov Halevy card and the amber strip on the Beatriz Salgado card, and their weight relative to the rest of their cards
finding: These two strips carry the only facts on the page that should change a decision, and both are the lowest-weight objects in their own card: the smallest type present, set below the 'Brought by' label immediately beneath them, on a 10% tint with a 30% ring. Then the pair are made structurally identical to each other — same radius, same fill alpha, same ring alpha, same position, same full width, same size — so hue alone has to carry the difference between 'the push actually failed' and 'a clock is running out'. And the hues are not at the same rung: the danger strip's text sits a step lighter than the warn strip's, so it reads as near-white on a faintly plum field and barely registers as red, while the amber reads vivid. The result inverts the system's own severity ranking. Squint the full page and the ageing notice is the loudest coloured object after the buttons, and the failure notice is a smudge — a reviewer skimming five cards will stop on the wrong one.
evidence: Crops of review--desktop-full.png at y=1178–1211 and y=1570–1604 side by side: the amber band's ring and text are plainly legible at a squint, the red band's are not. Both strips are 34px tall, both are the smallest type in their card, and in both cases the 14px 'Brought by' label sits directly below at higher contrast. On the squint pass the amber block is the second brightest mass on the page and the red block reads as neutral.
direction: Two moves. The strips need to outrank the definition list they sit above — as composed they are read last, when they are the reason the card is different from the four around it. And the two must sit at the same rung of the ramp so that hue is the only difference between them: bring the danger text up to the rung warn already uses, so red reads at least as loud as amber, not quieter.

where: the amber 'N students with this name are already on the roster' line at the foot of Ethan Nguyen's and Elena Salgado's child rows
finding: This is the question the whole screen exists to answer and the only door into the merge picker, and it is the one interactive object in the card with no affordance whatsoever — bare small amber text, no fill, no ring, no persistent underline, no disclosure mark — sitting inside a card where every other actionable thing is a filled, ringed rectangle. It reads as a caption on the row above it, a warning you are being told about rather than the control that resolves it. The hairline above it makes it worse: the rule runs the full 1096px of the row to separate a 300px sentence from a 240px name, which frames the line as a footnote appended to the row. Meanwhile the child's name above it is also a link with no static signal, so the row contains two interactive objects and looks like it contains none.
evidence: review--desktop-full.png, Ethan Nguyen's row: the amber sentence sits at x=284–584 under a border that spans x=285–1380. Compare the merge candidates it opens, which are seated buttons on ink-900 with a ring — the destination looks like a control and the door into it does not. Every other press target in the card ('Approve and add', 'Not ours') is a filled rectangle.
direction: Give the line the same seated, ringed treatment the merge candidates behind it already use, or at minimum a persistent underline and a disclosure mark, so it reads as the way in rather than as a caption. And size the hairline to the block it actually divides rather than to the full row.

where: the rule under every card header, and where it meets the coloured strips on the Dov Halevy and Beatriz Salgado cards
finding: The card body carries side and bottom padding but no top padding, so the header's rule sits 12px below the header's last line and 1px above the body's first — optically about 15px of air above it and 5px below. A rule that belongs to the header is glued to the body instead, and every card reads as if its header had been cropped short. On the two cards that open with a coloured strip it degrades further: the strip's top ring lands on exactly the same pixel row as the rule, so the grey rule runs into the strip's rounded corner and survives only as a 16px stub poking out on each side. That looks like a rendering seam, not a decision.
evidence: Card 1: description line box ends y=148, rule at y=160, dl line box starts y=161 (glyphs from 165). Card 4: header rule and the danger strip's top ring are both at y=1178; the crop at x=256–460 shows the grey rule terminating into the red corner curve.
direction: Give the body a top inset that matches its bottom one, so the rule closes the header rather than opening the body, and so the strips have room to be their own object instead of colliding with the divider.

where: the 'Brought by / Phone' definition list, and its relationship to the card title above it and the child names below it
finding: Four of the five cards title themselves with the guardian's name and then restate it verbatim one row down, so a two-row grid is carrying one new fact — the phone number. What remains of the list is a label column whose only remaining job is to size the value column, and it sizes it by accident: the width of the words 'Brought by' pushes the values to x=362, which is 29px right of the child names at x=333. That is a fourth left edge inside a card that already has three, and it lines up with nothing. Compounding it, the guardian's name appears in three near-adjacent treatments across the card — the title, the value, and the child rows are within two pixels of size and one weight step of each other — so at a squint the family and its members read at the same level and the card has no visible subject.
evidence: Left edges inside one card: 273 (title, dt), 285 (strip text, avatar), 333 (child names), 362 (dl values). 'Priya Nguyen' appears at 273 as the title and again at 362 as the value; same for Marta Okonjo, Dov Halevy and Beatriz Salgado. Total dl content width is 181px in a 1120px band.
direction: The definition list should carry only what the header does not — the number — which removes both the repetition and the label column that was misaligning the values. And the card title needs to step further away from the child names, so that the family reads as the container and the children as its contents.

where: the amber duplicate line inside Ethan Nguyen's child row
finding: It is a button element and inherits the browser's centre alignment. That is invisible on desktop, where it shrinks to its content, but at 390px it fills the row and wraps: the line breaks after 'on the' and leaves 'roster' alone and centred beneath, under a row where the avatar, the name and the grade all share a single left edge. A centred orphan in an otherwise left-aligned row is the most conspicuous misalignment on the phone frame, and it makes the most important sentence on the card look like an afterthought.
evidence: review--phone-fold.png, Ethan Nguyen's row: 'roster' sits alone, horizontally centred, while 'EN', 'Ethan Nguyen' and '6th grade · Peanuts — carries an EpiPen' are flush left on a common edge 8px above it.
direction: Left-align it to the same edge as the rest of the row's content, so the wrap reads as a paragraph and not as a caption.

where: the coloured strips against the child rows directly beneath them on the Dov Halevy and Beatriz Salgado cards
finding: The strip and the child rows are siblings in the same stack at the same inset, and they carry different corner radii — the strip's corners are visibly tighter than the rows'. Nothing about their nesting depth or role justifies the difference, so it reads as an accident and makes the strip look like a foreign object dropped into the card rather than one of its parts. It is the only place in the card where two things at the same level disagree about their own shape.
evidence: review--phone-full.png, Beatriz Salgado's card: the amber strip and the Tomás Salgado row below it start and end at the same x, but the strip's corner arc is about two-thirds the radius of the row's.
direction: Siblings at the same inset should share a radius. Match the strip to the rows.

where: the second line of Ethan Nguyen's child row — '6th grade · Peanuts — carries an EpiPen'
finding: The one medical fact on the screen is joined to the grade by a middle dot and set in the card's quietest token at its smallest size, which makes it typographically identical to '4th grade' on the row below — a fact of an entirely different kind, rendered the same way, as a continuation of the sentence rather than a thing in itself. Sixteen pixels below it and across a hairline, the name-collision note is amber and arrives first. Inside one row the composition ranks a possible duplicate above an EpiPen.
evidence: review--phone-fold.png: '6th grade · Peanuts — carries an EpiPen' is one uniform grey run at the row's smallest size; the amber line beneath it is the only coloured text in the card and is what the eye lands on.
direction: Break the allergy off the grade — its own line, and a step up the ink ramp — so it stops reading as more of the same sentence. Do not reach for another accent: warn is already doing two unrelated jobs in this card, marking both an expiring record and a name collision.
